permitted.text: On January 18, 2022 , we entered into a definitive agreement to acquire Activision Blizzard , Inc. (“Activision Blizzard” ) for $ 95 .00 per share in an all-cash transaction valued at $ 68 .7 billion, inclusive of Activision Blizzard’s net cash. The acquisition has been approved by Activision Blizzard’s shareholders, and we expect it to close in fiscal year 2023, subject to the satisfaction of certain regulatory approvals and other customary closing conditions.

On October 13, 2023, we completed our acquisition of Activision Blizzard for a total purchase price of $75.4 billion, consisting primarily of cash. The financial results of Activision Blizzard have been included in our consolidated financial statements since the date of the acquisition. Activision Blizzard is reported as part of our More Personal Computing segment.

In addition, at the Effective Time, subject to certain exceptions, unvested Activision Blizzard options and stock-based awards were assumed by Microsoft and converted into corresponding awards that are subject to shares of Microsoft common stock.
Operating expenses increased $3.8 billion or 6% driven by investments in cloud and AI engineering and Gaming, including the impact of the Activision Blizzard acquisition.

Earlier this month, we were thrilled to close our acquisition of Activision Blizzard, and we look forward to sharing
more in the coming months about how, together, we will bring the joy of gaming to more people around the world.

text:
## Where MSFT stood at the start of the window

The FY2020 10-K describes a company organised around cloud infrastructure and a single unifying mission: "Microsoft is a technology company whose mission is to empower every person and every organization on the planet to achieve more" [LANG-FY2020-65191b16]. The strategic frame is explicit and pre-AI: "the new era of the intelligent cloud and intelligent edge" [SP-FY2020-68ae8f40], executed against three research-and-development ambitions — reinventing productivity, building the cloud and edge platform, creating more personal computing [SP-FY2020-859252a8]. Reporting matched: "We operate our business and report our financial performance using three segments: Productivity and Business Processes, Intelligent Cloud, and More Personal Computing" [SEG-FY2020-1167ad3f]. AI appears, but as a data-derived advantage inside Azure rather than as the company's identity [SP-FY2020-27953e24]. Headcount was approximately 163,000, roughly 96,000 in the U.S. [HC-FY2020-e08216bd].

Two commitments made in that year set the terms for everything after. Management told investors capital spending would rise — "We expect capital expenditures to increase in coming years to support growth in our cloud offerings" [LANG-FY2020-be44cfd1] — and conceded the consequence: "The investments we are making in infrastructure and devices will continue to increase our operating costs and may decrease our operating margins" [LANG-FY2020-7f3daef6].

Governance was in transition. "Bill Gates, co-founder and member of the Board of Directors of Microsoft, resigned from the Board effective March 13, 2020" [EVT-FY2020-35f7d093], following the announced retirement of two directors of 2003 vintage [EVT-FY2020-0c6958a7]. Pay was the soft spot: at the December 4, 2019 annual meeting, say-on-pay drew 76.69% support [EVT-FY2020-c1ac7b65], which the proxy itself records as "At the 2019 Annual Meeting, 77% of the votes cast supported our advisory resolution on the compensation of our Named Executives" [LANG-FY2020-0215498c].

## The arc

**The self-description migrates from cloud to AI, and the margin admission migrates with it.** The mission sentence is stable to the character across FY2020, FY2021 and FY2022 [LANG-FY2020-65191b16, LANG-FY2021-ca92610f, LANG-FY2022-d8a32eb9]. What changes is the clause in front of it. By FY2023 the MD&A opens with "We are creating the platforms and tools, powered by artificial intelligence" [LANG-FY2023-46e80023]; FY2024 and FY2025 lead with an identical sentence naming AI in the first clause of the company's definition of itself [LANG-FY2024-ef3e7ad8, LANG-FY2025-f7d8f90f]. The cost disclosure tracks the same path word for word: the FY2020 sentence about "infrastructure and devices" [LANG-FY2020-7f3daef6, LANG-FY2022-fd0f8bad] becomes, from FY2023 onward, "The investments we are making in cloud and AI infrastructure and devices will continue to increase our operating costs and may decrease our operating margins" [LANG-FY2023-aee9457e, LANG-FY2024-608e151b, LANG-FY2025-be24791c]. The capex sentence escalates in parallel, adding AI infrastructure in FY2023 and AI training in FY2024 [LANG-FY2023-8691640e, LANG-FY2024-424e1912]. By FY2025 the warning has stopped being hypothetical: "Microsoft Cloud gross margin percentage decreased to 69% driven by the impact of scaling our AI infrastructure" [LANG-FY2025-c32e49cc], against a slight decline to 71% the year before [LANG-FY2024-62cc851d]. A second new disclosure arrives with the build: from FY2023 the filings state that "Our datacenters depend on the availability of permitted and buildable land, predictable energy, networking supplies, and servers, including graphics processing units" [LANG-FY2023-db44cac3, LANG-FY2024-b07c6ef6, LANG-FY2025-d38eef4d]. A software company began describing physical inputs as dependencies.

**Depreciation policy moved twice in the same direction as the build.** Effective FY2021, server lives went from three to four years and network equipment from two to four, which management estimated at $2.7 billion of operating income and $2.3 billion of net income [EVT-FY2020-1e636757, EVT-FY2021-74348aa6]. Effective FY2023, both went from four to six years, estimated at $3.7 billion of operating income and $3.0 billion of net income, or $0.40 per share [EVT-FY2022-e8bfc9ba, EVT-FY2023-2453e66e]. The stated reason each time is software efficiency and advances in technology, not earnings management [EVT-FY2022-e8bfc9ba]. The analytically important consequence is disclosed by management itself: in FY2021 gross margin percentage "decreased slightly" once the change is excluded [LANG-FY2021-78ab008f], in FY2022 the reported percentage fell and only rose a point after excluding the prior-year change [LANG-FY2022-fdd34974], and in FY2024 the Microsoft Cloud margin decline reverses to a slight increase on the same adjustment [LANG-FY2024-62cc851d]. Three of the window's margin narratives are legible only through the estimate change.

**Acquisitions escalated by an order of magnitude, and the rationales came in a register the 10-K does not use.** ZeniMax closed March 2021 at $8.1 billion into More Personal Computing [EVT-FY2021-5a713f8c]; Nuance was agreed at $19.7 billion [EVT-FY2021-311ce44a] and closed March 2022 at $18.8 billion into Intelligent Cloud [EVT-FY2022-d82ea211]; Activision Blizzard was agreed at $68.7 billion in January 2022 [EVT-FY2022-a94337e6], extended through October 18, 2023 to address regulatory concerns [EVT-FY2023-cd0e43dc], and closed at a purchase price of $75.4 billion into More Personal Computing [EVT-FY2024-e9d208cf, EVT-FY2024-c72a6719]. The strategic claims sit in Regulation FD voluntary disclosure rather than in periodic reports: on Nuance, that the deal doubles the healthcare provider TAM to nearly $500 billion [QA-FY2021-caf4abc6] and that "AI is technology's most important priority, and healthcare is its most urgent application" [QA-FY2021-edfb4a6b] — a formulation that predates the AI framing of the FY2023 10-K by two years; on Activision, that it "will provide building blocks for the metaverse" [QA-FY2022-b598943b] and would make Microsoft the third-largest gaming company by revenue [QA-FY2022-8856672c]. The metaverse framing did reach Item 1 in FY2022 — "enabling metaverse experiences at all layers of our stack" [SP-FY2022-7da446a1] — and then does not recur in the FY2023–FY2025 strategic-priority extractions in this pack, where the same slot is occupied by Copilot and agents [SP-FY2023-650de626, SP-FY2024-9b2c9b6f, SP-FY2025-a9ac2962]. Reg FD material carries full weight here, but the register matters: these were management's unaudited framings at announcement, not disclosures the periodic reports later repeated.

**Capital returns were rebalanced toward the build.** Repurchases rose from $19.7 billion (126 million shares) in FY2020 to $28.0 billion (95 million) in FY2022 [EVT-FY2020-93519ac9, EVT-FY2022-95bf4115], then fell to $18.4 billion, $12.0 billion and $13.0 billion in FY2023–FY2025 [EVT-FY2023-e746c1c4, EVT-FY2024-779b6ad5, EVT-FY2025-92f42551]. Dividends moved the other way: quarterly $0.62 in FY2022, $0.68 and $20.2 billion in FY2023, $22.3 billion in FY2024 [EVT-FY2022-d35c1783, EVT-FY2023-acbab3d7, EVT-FY2024-2a84b3d4]. Buybacks roughly halved from peak while the dividend grew and capex commitments escalated; the filings state each fact but offer no linking explanation, so the trade-off is inference rather than disclosure.

**Cost discipline is a stated priority, but the headcount record is not a clean retrenchment.** Employment ran approximately 163,000, 181,000, 221,000, 221,000, 228,000 and 228,000 across FY2020–FY2025 [HC-FY2020-e08216bd, HC-FY2021-b24eab72, HC-FY2022-e5fe1437, HC-FY2023-116418a0, HC-FY2024-3cda7ba5, HC-FY2025-8041c917]. The January 2023 announcement produced a $1.2 billion charge including $800 million of severance and reduced the workforce by roughly 10,000 jobs, under 5% of the base [EVT-FY2023-7530a8cb], accompanied by a salary freeze [SP-FY2023-73c249dc] and unusually plain language: "While we eliminated roles in some areas, we will continue to hire in key strategic areas," with capital and talent moving to secular growth "while divesting in other areas" [LANG-FY2023-78583354]. Operating leverage then appears as a standing letter priority in FY2023 and FY2024 [SP-FY2023-d99d40a9, SP-FY2024-1238e7aa]. Note the evidence limit: shareholder letters exist in this pack only for FY2023, FY2024 and FY2025 [per the pack's letter constraint], so any apparent change in leadership voice at the FY2022/FY2023 boundary may be a missing document.

**Executive pay is the most legible record of which priorities were actually being paid for.** The FY2020 performance-share metrics spread weight across Commercial Cloud revenue and subscribers, Teams, Xbox Game Pass, Surface and LinkedIn [INC-FY2020-79e68f2d, INC-FY2020-1a29d28c, INC-FY2020-c3add9b3, INC-FY2020-2aaaba97, INC-FY2020-a2fa7621, INC-FY2020-455c6902]. FY2021 doubled the Teams weight with a stated reason — "With the growing importance of Teams on our business strategy, we increased the weight for Teams Monthly Active Usage metric" [LANG-FY2021-2c70b149]. By FY2024 both Teams usage and Windows monthly active devices were removed and 70% of the weight sat on two cloud-revenue growth metrics, the committee's stated reason being "a significant business shift to AI" [LANG-FY2024-ee0a5f0b, INC-FY2024-bfead9e0, INC-FY2024-9e059050]. FY2025 broadened the advertising metric into Consumer Services revenue growth and dropped LinkedIn sessions as double-counted [LANG-FY2025-6b61d4a4, LANG-FY2024-4ac09c86, INC-FY2025-64d2afa8]. In parallel, CEO equity went from 50% performance-based to 70% for FY2021 and to 100% for FY2022 at a $50,000,000 target [INC-FY2020-4ae39800, LANG-FY2021-5cb1a563, LANG-FY2022-eedd3d56, LANG-FY2022-f47c8dc1], with the FY2021 changes attributed directly to investor feedback [LANG-FY2020-4a365693, LANG-FY2021-5989e1f9]. Support followed the redesign, then wobbled: 94.72% at the December 2, 2020 meeting [VOTE-FY2020-1a34f291], 95.45% at the November 30, 2021 meeting [VOTE-FY2021-3058cd7e], 88.84% at the December 13, 2022 meeting [VOTE-FY2022-b2f5ae1c] — the first year of the $50 million award — then 93.77% (December 7, 2023) and 91.34% (December 10, 2024) [VOTE-FY2023-a4d26e68, VOTE-FY2024-7df37ae7].

**Security is elevated from a risk factor to a paid priority, and the mechanism is visible.** The Secure Future Initiative launched November 2023 and was expanded in May 2024 [LANG-FY2024-a39aa42c], with security made "a dimension of rewards decisions across the Company" [LANG-FY2024-b34a3e5a]. Most concretely, the board reduced the CEO's cash incentive by more than half against the formulaic outcome — "it was appropriate to reduce Mr. Nadella's cash incentive award" [LANG-FY2024-cb5c341b]. A Security category then entered the FY2025 incentive plan at 10% CEO weight [INC-FY2024-4e3b9f27, LANG-FY2025-646f92ff], scored at 140% [INC-FY2025-224f0cb4]. Item 1 now states "We prioritize security above all else" [SP-FY2025-b7139777], and the FY2025 letter asserts "Security and quality are non-negotiable" alongside 34,000 full-time-engineer equivalents dedicated to the work [LANG-FY2025-5853a64b, LANG-FY2025-ad323cdc]. Consistently, the largest Item 1A rewrite in the FY2024 diff was the information-technology security factor [RISK-FY2024-102d3e1b].

**Reporting was recomposed under stable segment names.** The names in the FY2025 10-K are the same three as in FY2020 [SEG-FY2020-1167ad3f, SEG-FY2025-0c3754fd], but the contents moved: commercial Microsoft 365 was brought into Productivity and Business Processes effective FY2025, with prior periods recast [EVT-FY2025-a527f1bf, SEG-FY2025-23694750], and Windows OEM and Devices were combined into one metric [SEG-FY2025-62225083]. The Regulation FD presentation is more specific about what this does to the headline number: with Enterprise Mobility + Security and Power BI per-user revenue moved out, the "Azure metric now more closely aligns to consumption business" [QA-FY2025-946672a5], while Nuance Enterprise moved to Dynamics and Copilot Pro to search and news advertising [QA-FY2025-85d9203c, QA-FY2025-2dd3fa4a] — each justified by the same recurring phrase, "to align to how the business is managed" [QA-FY2025-8fc0cbf5]. The practical effect is that post-recast Azure is a narrower, consumption-weighted line than the pre-recast one, and earlier metric changes compound it: commercial cloud renamed Microsoft Cloud in FY2022, Surface expanded into Devices in FY2023, Microsoft Cloud revised in FY2024 [SEG-FY2022-77ccf0fc, SEG-FY2023-73774bfa, EVT-FY2024-24da11a9].

**Tax exposure grew from an audit to the largest single quantified contingency in the pack.** Microsoft settled a portion of the 2004–2013 audits for $1.7 billion in Q2 FY2021 [EVT-FY2021-1ae01eae]; on September 26, 2023 the IRS issued notices seeking $28.9 billion plus penalties and interest on intercompany transfer pricing [EVT-FY2024-2e0a47cf, EVT-FY2025-b33b8831]. Management's language is unusually combative and explicitly open-ended: "We disagree with the proposed adjustments and will vigorously contest the NOPAs… We do not expect a final resolution of these issues in the next 12 months" [LANG-FY2024-44cdda28]. Around it sit Pillar Two from FY2025, a 14% GILTI rate from FY2027 under legislation enacted July 4, 2025, and a final $4.4 billion TCJA installment due in Q1 FY2026 [EVT-FY2025-8a4c8d0e, EVT-FY2025-c26b2f68, EVT-FY2025-ed7423c8].

**The shareholder ballot re-pointed at AI.** The November 30, 2021 meeting produced a management-opposed proposal that passed, on workplace sexual-harassment policy effectiveness at 77.97% [VOTE-FY2021-efd1c5f5]. By the December 7, 2023 meeting the ballot included AI misinformation at 21.16% [VOTE-FY2023-5a8efc12]; at December 10, 2024, AI data-sourcing accountability drew 36.19% — the highest non-management proposal that year [VOTE-FY2024-75e0b946]. At the meeting reported in the 8-K filed December 8, 2025, AI data-usage oversight drew 13.36% while human-rights-hotspot data operations declined to 27.48% from 32.03% and 33.57% in the two prior meetings [VOTE-FY2025-4876a0f8, VOTE-FY2025-1b4918ba, VOTE-FY2024-11ca5541, VOTE-FY2023-311fea9a]. The subject matter of dissent followed the strategy.

**Board and executive changes are recorded thinly.** MacGregor and Mason were elected December 7, 2023 [LEAD-FY2024-8183a97e, LEAD-FY2024-597f130a]; Rainey was elected at the meeting reported December 8, 2025 [VOTE-FY2025-ab8a997b]. Christopher Young resigned as Executive Vice President, Business Development, Strategy, and Ventures on January 22, 2025, with no reason stated [LEAD-FY2025-7123b34a]. The proxy signature block shifts from Thompson and Nadella to Peterson and Nadella between FY2022 and FY2023 [BRD-FY2022-dfe6e54e, BRD-FY2023-6412443d] — but these board facts are low-confidence in this pack, their source-section boundaries unverified, and no role change is stated anywhere in it.

## Where it stands now

Management's most recent statement of priority is three-part and puts security first: "three core business priorities as our North Star: security, quality, and AI innovation" [SP-FY2025-93e18460], executed under a repeated pacing formula — "think in decades but execute in quarters" [LANG-FY2025-b391d575]. The AI position is stated as infrastructure plus Copilots and agents [SP-FY2025-a9ac2962], with more than 400 datacenters in 70 regions [SP-FY2025-7ae64643], a new Wisconsin facility claimed as the world's most powerful AI datacenter [LANG-FY2025-ca2c1c15], sovereign cloud offerings [SP-FY2025-18f626d5], and internal adoption as "Customer Zero" [SP-FY2025-b6aad44f]. The letter reports revenue of $281.7 billion up 15%, operating income of $128.5 billion up 17%, and Azure past $75 billion up 34% [LANG-FY2025-5e3f656f] — voluntary shareholder-letter figures, not audited statements in this pack.

The FY2025 10-K describes the OpenAI relationship in its own section for the first time in the window: a partnership originating in 2019, reciprocal revenue sharing, and rights over OpenAI's intellectual property "including models and infrastructure, for integration into our products" [LANG-FY2025-ee136163]. The same filing names it as an earnings drag: "Other, net primarily reflects net recognized losses on equity method investments, including OpenAI" [LANG-FY2025-81175065]. Elsewhere the consumer picture is mixed — a January 2025 Microsoft 365 Consumer price increase lifting revenue per user [EVT-FY2025-9d90f5b3] against a blunt "Xbox hardware revenue decreased 25% driven by lower volume of consoles sold" [LANG-FY2025-48edf2ad].

What management chose to newly disclose as risk is, notably, nothing. In the FY2025-versus-FY2024 Item 1A diff in this pack, no risk factor was added or removed; a single factor was reworded, "Other digital safety abuses," at 78.8% body similarity, with the other seven tracked factors substantially unchanged [RISK-FY2025-a378afcf, RISK-FY2025-762f1c0f, RISK-FY2025-03ce1160]. The tracked set covers competition, security and platform-abuse factors rather than the whole of Item 1A, so this is a statement about that set. Within it, the year's genuinely new exposures surface in MD&A rather than as new risk headings — trade policy and tariffs are discussed as potential drivers of supply-chain and cost volatility [LANG-FY2025-1aa54f85], and the physical dependency language on land, energy and GPUs remains in MD&A [LANG-FY2025-d38eef4d]. Management escalated AI capital intensity substantially without adding a risk-factor heading for it.

## What the filings raise but do not answer

**The repurchase authorization reappears without an authorizing event.** As of June 30, 2024, $10.3 billion remained of the $60 billion program [EVT-FY2024-779b6ad5]; as of June 30, 2025, $57.3 billion remained of a $60 billion program after $13.0 billion of buybacks [EVT-FY2025-92f42551]. A new authorization is the only reading that reconciles these, and the pack contains no such event.

**Capex is committed to repeatedly and never sized.** Every year states that capital expenditures will increase [LANG-FY2020-be44cfd1, LANG-FY2023-8691640e, LANG-FY2024-424e1912], and FY2025 states the margin consequence [LANG-FY2025-be24791c, LANG-FY2025-c32e49cc], but the pack contains no capex figure for any year. The central financial question of the window — how much the AI build costs and what it earns — cannot be answered from this evidence.

**The OpenAI economics are described qualitatively only.** Reciprocal revenue sharing, IP rights, exclusivity and equity-method losses are all named [LANG-FY2025-ee136163, LANG-FY2025-81175065, SP-FY2024-98108cc9] with no amounts, no term, and no loss quantification.

**The Activision consideration is not reconciled.** Announced at $68.7 billion inclusive of net cash [EVT-FY2022-a94337e6], recorded at a $75.4 billion purchase price [EVT-FY2024-e9d208cf], with unvested awards assumed and converted [EVT-FY2024-db8cdea3]. The pack does not bridge the two figures. Nor does it quantify the result: the only FY2025 line touching the deal's effect names it as one contributor, alongside cloud and AI engineering and Gaming investment, to a $3.8 billion or 6% increase in operating expenses, with no revenue effect quantified [EVT-FY2025-738145c1], and the FY2023 letter gave the largest deal in the window two sentences deferring detail to "the coming months" [LANG-FY2023-268d7db2].

**The security failure behind the CEO's pay cut is never described.** The board cut the CEO bonus by more than half for cybersecurity reasons [LANG-FY2024-cb5c341b] and stood up SFI in response to a "threat landscape" [LANG-FY2024-a39aa42c]. No incident, breach, scope or cost appears anywhere in the pack. An analyst cannot size what was being answered for.

**The recast is asserted but not shown.** FY2025 states prior periods were recast [SEG-FY2025-23694750], and the Regulation FD presentation insists it made "mechanical updates only to our outlook" [QA-FY2025-dca2c1c3]. No restated prior-period figures are in the pack, so the claim that the recomposition changed presentation and not expectations cannot be tested — and Azure growth across the FY2024/FY2025 boundary cannot be compared on a like basis.

**Flat headcount and an expanded-scope operating model are not connected.** Employment is approximately 228,000 in both FY2024 and FY2025 [HC-FY2024-3cda7ba5, HC-FY2025-8041c917] while the letter describes a way of working that "expands job scopes, reduces handoffs" and pre-emptively denies the obvious reading: "This isn't just about driving efficiency" [SP-FY2025-5d97596a, LANG-FY2025-ffbbe631]. The pack records no FY2025 reduction event and no hiring-versus-attrition split, so whether flat headcount reflects substitution or stasis is unresolved.

**Two smaller items sit unresolved in the record itself.** The expected Cruise impairment of approximately $800 million, explicitly excluded from prior guidance [EVT-FY2025-5c9375b6], has no final recorded amount in the pack. And the filings are internally inconsistent in places the pack flags rather than fixes: the 8-K reporting the 2023 annual meeting states a December 7, 2022 date in its own text [EVT-FY2024-2590aa4d] while the meeting is dated December 7, 2023 elsewhere in the same filing's vote records [LEAD-FY2024-8183a97e]; and one auditor-ratification vote carries a heading naming fiscal year 2023 against item text naming fiscal year 2024 [VOTE-FY2023-cb33864e]. Separately, the pack records unresolved date conflicts for several director rows, including Nadella, Thompson, Hoffman and Walmsley, where two filings give different dates and neither is presented as correct.
